candidateRows: Change and essentially ordered causal chains require a transcendent actual source identified as God.
This presentation of Aquinas's first way is one of the affirmative's principal natural-theology proofs and directly supports God's existence.
Egnor begins his affirmative case by presenting several Thomistic proofs, first reasoning from change, actuality, and instrumental causal chains.
The existence of contingent things requires at least one necessary being rather than universal contingency.
The contingency argument supplies a distinct metaphysical route from ordinary dependent existence to a necessary foundation.
After briefly identifying a causation-based second way, Egnor presents the third way from contingent existence to necessary existence.
Stable lawlike behavior by mindless natural objects implies a directing mind and purposeful design.
The teleological fifth way is a principal affirmative proof linking natural regularity directly to intelligent guidance.
Egnor argues that inanimate entities reliably follow natural laws despite lacking knowledge of their prescribed behavior.
Mind-independent universals and propositions are best grounded as contents of the divine intellect.
The Augustinian proof offers a separate ontological argument that uses the apparent reality of universals to infer God.
Egnor maintains that mathematical objects, propositions, justice, and mercy have reality independent of individual human minds.
The demand for sufficient explanations ultimately requires a self-explanatory source outside nature, namely God.
This proof applies a universal explanatory principle to existence and derives an ultimate explanation beyond nature.
Egnor presents a rationalist argument associated with Leibniz, claiming that existing things cannot simply lack any explanation.
Objective moral obligations require a divine intellect and therefore provide strong evidence that God exists.
The argument from moral law directly addresses both God's existence and whether objective morality can survive atheism.
Egnor argues that judgments about acts such as killing innocent people are objectively true rather than matters of preference.
Theistic claims bear the burden of proof, while undefined or unfalsifiable gods cannot rationally be affirmed.
This establishes the negative side's governing burden-of-proof position and challenges the tenability of typical God claims.
Egnor's affirmative claim that his natural-theology arguments establish that God exists.
Dillahunty distinguishes disbelief from proving universal nonexistence and argues that no assessable divine ontology has been supplied.
Withholding belief when evidence is insufficient is a rational, revisable conclusion rather than personal incredulity.
The move supplies the epistemic standard by which the negative side rejects the affirmative proofs without claiming certainty.
Egnor's contention that atheists lack adequate answers and that his proofs are effectively irrefutable.
Dillahunty separates disbelief from the fallacy of inferring nonexistence merely from disbelief, then advocates evidence-responsive tentativeness.
Classical divine attributes cannot be demonstrated or distinguished from merely extraordinary but finite capacities.
The challenge attacks the inference from an unexplained or powerful cause to the specific God required by classical theism.
Egnor's natural-theology inferences from causal, explanatory, teleological, and moral premises to God.
Dillahunty tests attributes associated with classical theism and argues that limited observers cannot verify maximal knowledge or power.
A detectable God capable of producing belief should be demonstrable, yet persistent nonbelief supports withholding assent.
This divine-hiddenness argument directly supports the negative conclusion for interventionist and revelation-seeking conceptions of God.
Egnor's assertion that natural evidence and multiple philosophical proofs provide strong reason to affirm God.
Dillahunty limits his conclusion to relevant popular gods, defends nonbelief as the default, and cites absent convincing disclosure.
Reports of divine communication are unreliable because believers protect God from falsification even when purported messages prove harmful or false.
The move directly challenges experiential revelation as evidence for God by exposing its susceptibility to error and belief-preserving rationalization.
The earlier theistic reliance on religious experience and purported encounters with the divine as evidence.
During his opening case, Dillahunty uses a harmful vaccination story and broader reports of divine messages to argue that conviction does not demonstrate truth.
God has not been adequately defined or demonstrated, so disbelief remains tentative and rationally revisable upon valid evidence.
This passage states the con side's direct answer to the motion and specifies the evidential condition under which that answer would change.
Egnor's opening claim that Thomistic arguments establish an entity appropriately identified as God.
Dillahunty argues that the debate supplied neither a usable definition nor physical evidence or sound argument, then states his provisional conclusion that God does not exist.
Atheists share the burden of proof because nature supplies extensive evidence of an underlying mind and historical intellectual consensus favors theism.
The move contests the con side's epistemic framework and asserts that both sides must defend their conclusions about the evidence in nature.
Dillahunty's claim that disbelief is the default and that the proponent alone bears the burden of demonstrating God.
At the start of open discussion, Egnor distinguishes God from fanciful beings, invokes historical theism, and rejects the idea that atheists need not defend their position.
Observed causal chains within the universe do not establish equivalent causation beyond it, and timeless existence is conceptually incoherent.
The argument attacks the extrapolation from ordinary causation to a transcendent cause, a foundational step in the offered cosmological proofs.
Egnor's appeal to Aquinas's causal way as an argument capable of demonstrating God's existence.
Pressed on Aquinas's second way, Dillahunty identifies causation as its subject but denies that causal behavior inside observable reality licenses conclusions outside time or the universe.
An instrumental regress of change requires a purely actual first mover because possibilities cannot actualize themselves without an existing source of actuality.
This is the pro side's developed presentation of a principal Thomistic proof intended to infer a first mover identified with God.
Dillahunty's demand that Egnor present and defend one substantive argument rather than list abbreviated proofs.
Egnor develops the first way from observed change through potency, actuality, instrumental causal series, and the claimed impossibility of an infinite regress without pure actuality.
Even if a first cause were needed, the argument neither identifies it as God nor demonstrates a timeless thinking agent or mental creator of descriptive natural laws.
The reply targets the inferential gap between a first cause and God while also disputing the coherence and evidential basis of a timeless divine mind.
Egnor's first-way conclusion that a purely actual prime mover terminates instrumental regress and is what people call God.
Dillahunty argues that causal reasoning is temporally conditioned, that a first cause reveals no divine attributes, and that natural laws are descriptions rather than products requiring a mind.
Infinite instrumental regress is impossible without prior actuality, and natural theology infers God through the same explanatory structure used in science.
The passage defends both the crucial no-regress premise and the methodological legitimacy of inferring a transcendent explanation from natural observations.
Dillahunty's challenge to demonstrate the impossibility of infinite regress and his objection that the proposed cause lacks evidential support.

Egnor says a series consisting only of unrealized possibilities could produce no change, then characterizes the resulting inference to actuality as structurally continuous with scientific explanation.
Inference to the best explanation cannot legitimately include an undemonstrated supernatural candidate merely because an observation still lacks a known explanation.
This reply challenges the methodological bridge from explanatory inference to God by requiring independent grounds for admitting supernatural explanations as candidates.
Egnor's assertion that scientific explanation and proofs of God's existence employ the same logical structure.
Dillahunty accepts that science can use abductive reasoning but argues that candidate explanations must first be demonstrated as possible rather than supplemented with magic.
Scientific cosmology itself invokes an undefined, non-natural singularity, showing that explanation may transcend nature without ceasing to be scientific.
The argument supplies the pro side's concrete counterexample to the claim that science may never consider explanations beyond demonstrable natural entities.
Dillahunty's contention that abductive inquiry may not include undemonstrated or supernatural explanatory candidates.
Egnor characterizes the Big Bang singularity as undefined by general relativity and outside nature, then argues that science routinely uses such transcendent inferences.
Ignorance about the Big Bang does not make a supernatural explanation plausible, which must still be independently demonstrated rather than inserted into an evidential gap.
The move states the con side's core objection to natural-theological gap filling and preserves the demand for testable evidence despite incomplete science.
Egnor's claim that cosmological singularities are supernatural and show science legitimately transcending nature in its explanations.
Dillahunty argues that lacking a current natural explanation licenses an admission of ignorance, not a supernatural replacement, drawing an analogy to abandoned divine accounts of lightning.
Big Bang cosmology neither establishes nor refutes God, and unexplained features of the universe do not justify inserting a divine explanation.
This directly contests the use of cosmological uncertainty as evidence for God and addresses the debate's central burden-of-proof dispute.
Egnor's contention that a cosmological singularity is supernatural and therefore supports reasoning beyond nature.
After being pressed to define a singularity, Dillahunty describes it as a model-dependent abstraction and argues that ignorance about cosmology licenses humility rather than a divine inference.
Science can infer an extranatural cause from natural effects, just as cosmology treats singularities that lie outside ordinary nature.
The move defends natural theology against the methodological objection that scientific reasoning cannot support a supernatural conclusion.
Dillahunty's claim that unexplained natural phenomena cannot warrant the insertion of a supernatural explanation.
Egnor argues that singularities are outside nature yet scientifically discussed, then generalizes that observation of natural effects can support inference to an extranatural cause.
Science is methodologically naturalistic, and supernatural explanations remain outside science until their existence, detectability, and operation can be demonstrated.
This supplies the skeptical standard governing whether natural theology can count as scientific evidence and directly bears on the asserted burden of proof.
Egnor's accusation that Dillahunty uses science as a crutch and his claim that science routinely appeals beyond nature.
Dillahunty distinguishes methodological naturalism from philosophical materialism and says science uses natural explanations while remaining open to demonstrable supernatural phenomena.
Aquinas's Five Ways qualify as scientific inductive arguments because they begin with observations in nature and infer God as the best explanation.
The move directly defends the motion's Thomistic proofs by locating their evidential method within the same inductive pattern used in empirical science.
Dillahunty's objection that Aquinas's Five Ways are philosophical arguments rather than scientific ones.
Egnor says deductive logic alone cannot establish existence, whereas Aquinas begins with natural experience and follows an inductive sequence to a supernatural best explanation.
Unknown cosmic origins should remain unknown rather than be assigned to God, while moral judgments can be understood as evaluations of consequences relative to goals.
The response states the skeptical alternative on both cosmological ignorance and morality, addressing two principal lines offered for the existence of God.
Egnor's opening questions about creation from nothing, the cause of natural laws, and the existence of evil.
Dillahunty says he does not know what caused the Big Bang, treats natural laws as extant properties, and explains evil through human labeling and goal-relative harm or benefit.
If moral wrongness is objective and independent of human opinion, an objective moral law points to a divine intellect as its source.
This is the debate's core moral argument for God, connecting the asserted objectivity of moral law directly to the existence of a divine mind.
Dillahunty's account of evil as human evaluation of actions by their consequences for adopted goals.
Egnor reframes the issue from why evil exists to whether anything is objectively wrong, arguing that independence from human opinion requires a divine intellectual ground.
Once morality is grounded in the well-being of thinking creatures, objective physical facts can determine whether actions advance or frustrate that standard.
The move offers a secular account of moral objectivity and thereby challenges the claim that objective moral evaluation requires a divine intellect.
Egnor's claim that without a divine moral law judgments of good and evil reduce merely to human opinion.
Dillahunty rejects cultural relativism, proposes well-being as morality's foundation, and analogizes objective moral assessment to factual assessments made within models of health.
Goal-relative moral assessments can be objective, whereas invoking God supplies no identifiable external standard or demonstrated reason anyone should accept it.
This sharpens the secular rebuttal by distinguishing objective assessment from absolute foundations and redirects the evidential burden toward the alleged divine standard.
Egnor's demand for an unconditional answer about objective wrongness and his question about the mind from which morality originates.
Dillahunty argues that right and wrong require a stated standard, permits objective conclusions relative to well-being, and says Egnor cannot identify or justify God's alleged standard.
A divinely impressed moral code is evidenced by people's felt moral obligation and their willingness to sacrifice personal interests or even their lives.
The move provides Egnor's experiential evidence for divine moral law, a necessary premise in his argument from objective morality to God.
Dillahunty's challenge to demonstrate that God has written a moral code on anyone's heart and to identify its content.
Egnor says all humans experience a moral code that can oppose convenience and self-interest, citing sacrifices made in service of moral duty as supporting evidence.
Self-sacrificial behavior does not establish a God-given moral code because altruism can have social, psychological, or selfish motivations that must be distinguished.
The response attacks the evidential bridge from sacrifice to divine authorship by supplying competing natural explanations for the same observed behavior.
Egnor's claim that costly self-sacrifice is evidence of an objective moral code written on the human heart.
Dillahunty denies a universal feeling, argues that societies reward sacrifice and people may seek acclaim, and requires distinguishing genuine altruism from strategically selfish conduct.
Altruistic conduct requires only a belief that an action is right and therefore cannot establish that an objective religious doctrine is true.
The move directly contests the claimed inference from self-sacrificial behavior to an objectively real, divinely grounded moral law.
Egnor's claim that genuine self-sacrifice evidences an objective moral law written on human hearts.
After distinguishing genuine from self-interested altruism, Dillahunty argues that sincere conduct tracks what an agent believes, not whether the believed doctrine is objectively real.
Objective moral laws do not exist as independent things, and merely believing in such a code neither identifies its content nor establishes its truth.
This directly addresses the debate's central dispute over whether objective moral law exists independently and supports an inference to God.
Egnor's demand for an ontological answer about objective moral laws and his examples of acts he regards as objectively wrong.

Dillahunty denies ontologically independent moral laws, separates moral convictions from proof of a code's content, and characterizes Egnor's desired explanations as fallacious grounds for Catholicism.
Atheism concerns belief in God and by itself entails no comprehensive doctrine about morality, purpose, cosmology, or how a person must live.
The move rejects a major premise of Egnor's critique by denying that atheism carries the moral and metaphysical commitments attributed to it.
Egnor's assertion that Dillahunty does not truly live as an atheist and that atheists share specified metaphysical beliefs.

Dillahunty defines atheism narrowly by reference to God-belief, distinguishes his personal views about purpose from necessary atheist commitments, and identifies Egnor's exclusion as a no-true-atheist error.
Expecting fair debate conduct rests on the participants' shared convention, not on an external divine moral standard, and is consistent with atheism.
This supplies a concrete secular basis for normative expectations and directly rebuts the claim that atheists implicitly rely on theistic objective morality.
Egnor's claim that Dillahunty's appeal to fairness shows atheists live like theists and rely on objective moral standards.
Dillahunty argues that fairness in the exchange derives from a voluntary agreement to share time under moderation, so enforcing that agreement requires no appeal to God-grounded morality.
Human existence, moral awareness, and the stable regularity of nature jointly point toward a creator, a moral source, and a physical lawgiver.
The move succinctly presents multiple natural-theology grounds offered as positive evidence that God exists, directly addressing the debate motion.
Answering what evidence could reach someone isolated from religious teaching, Egnor appeals to contingency, moral experience, and natural regularity as signs of divine agency.
Absent evidence about the cosmos before the earliest accessible physical era, one should not infer creation and may provisionally allow that some cosmos always existed.
This challenges cosmological arguments for God by disputing that current evidence establishes an absolute beginning requiring a supernatural cause.

Dillahunty distinguishes the observable expansion history from claims about an ultimate beginning, treats both beginning and eternality as requiring demonstration, and rejects unsupported causal explanations.
Shared secular interests can ground social cooperation to limit harm, while disagreement and antisocial conduct occur regardless of belief in God or religion.
The move provides a practical secular account of moral convergence and social restraint, opposing the claim that workable morality requires theism.
Egnor's contention that concepts such as harm and health make little sense without objective, theistically grounded morality.

Dillahunty notes substantial overlap between theists and atheists, rejects universalized moral intuitions, acknowledges harmful agents, and proposes cooperative institutions based on shared interests.
Evil is a privation of goodness inherent in finite creation, and God permits it for greater goods including free agency, moral action, and character formation.
The move answers a major objection to God's existence by offering a privation account and reasons a good God could permit moral and natural evil.
Egnor distinguishes evil from an independently existing substance, links finitude with deficient goodness, and argues that permitted suffering can enable freedom and character-building goods.
Change occurs only within time, but causation can originate outside time because a genuine first cause cannot itself belong to the temporal causal network.
This refines the Thomistic causal argument at the heart of the debate by distinguishing temporal change from the agency of a first cause.
The questioner's objection that Egnor's earlier reference to simultaneous change outside time was conceptually incoherent.
Egnor accepts that change depends on time but maintains that causal initiation need not, arguing that a first cause would cease to be first if situated within time's network of causes.

Morality is constructed around an agreed foundation that permits objective assessments, and appealing to God merely substitutes another rejectable foundation without solving secular morality's problems.
This is a compact restatement of the con side's central moral case and directly denies that divine grounding supplies a superior objective foundation.

Dillahunty identifies moral argumentation as especially recurrent, distinguishes constructed foundations from objective evaluations made relative to them, and argues that divine authority adds no solution to disagreement.
The Christian account of atonement remains an unexplained list of assertions rather than an intelligible reconciliation of justice and mercy.
The move challenges whether a major Christian doctrine supplies an actual explanation, directly bearing on the intelligibility and evidential force of the theistic case.
Egnor's claim that Christ paying humanity's debt reconciles divine justice with divine mercy.
Egnor has just presented the incarnation and atonement as Christianity's resolution of the tension between perfect justice and perfect mercy.
Scientific papers treating general-relativistic singularities discuss extranatural objects because the governing equations become infinite there.
The answer supports Egnor's disputed claim that scientific practice can describe realities beyond ordinary nature, a premise relevant to his natural-theology case.
The challenge asking which scientific papers mention supernatural things when discussing singularities.
A questioner asks Egnor to identify scientific literature that invokes supernatural entities or treats singularities as part of a scientific hypothesis.
Morality need not be objective by definition, because objective and subjective identify distinguishable categories of moral judgment rather than morality and nonmorality.
The move directly contests the definitional premise behind Egnor's moral argument, denying that removing objectivity necessarily removes morality itself.
Egnor's answer that morality without objectivity is merely subjective opinion and therefore is not morality.
After a question asks whether removing the word objective makes morality less moral, Egnor identifies morality with objectivity and dismisses subjectivity as opinion.
Atheism is a single position on one issue, not a predictive belief system; skepticism, humanism, and secular ethics supply separate epistemic and moral commitments.
The distinction rebuts attempts to assign atheism a comprehensive worldview and clarifies which commitments actually support Dillahunty's epistemology and secular morality.
The question's framing of atheism as a system of belief that could make predictions.
A viewer asks whether the debate should instead compare the predictive success of atheism understood as a system of belief.
Atheism is a substantive metaphysical perspective with associated commitments about nature, God, purpose, and moral accountability rather than a solitary lack of belief.
The move disputes Dillahunty's account of the con position and argues that atheism carries broad consequences relevant to cosmology, purpose, and morality.
Dillahunty's claim that atheism is only one position on one issue and has no predictive belief system.
Dillahunty has separated atheism from his skepticism, humanism, and secular ethics while criticizing blanket descriptions of Catholic or atheist belief.
Morality by its nature refers to standards outside human opinion, and reducing moral judgments to evolved opinion yields unacceptable consequences for plainly wrongful acts.
This is a direct defense of the moral-law component of the theistic case, asserting objectivity and challenging an evolutionary or emotivist reduction of moral obligation.
The suggestion that humans evolved a tendency to project emotional moral oughts as though they were objectively binding.
A viewer proposes that apparent objective duties may be evolved projections of emotion rather than evidence of genuinely mind-independent moral standards.
Appealing to a god does not solve disagreement between moral systems, while secular morality can seek consensus through discussion, debate, and evidence.
The move challenges the claimed justificatory advantage of divine morality and argues that observed conduct cannot demonstrate that God inscribed a shared moral code.
The challenge that differing objective moral codes lack an ultimate justification capable of determining which code is correct.
A viewer asks how competing moral codes can be adjudicated without ultimate justification, prompting comparison between religious and secular moral systems.
Knowledge of God is interpersonal like knowledge within marriage or friendship and therefore can transcend scientific testing or publicly demonstrable proof.
The move supplies Egnor's answer to the demand for public demonstration by locating warranted theistic knowledge in personal relationship rather than impersonal scientific proof.
Dillahunty's claim that Egnor cannot demonstrate that God wrote a moral code on his or anyone else's heart.
Dillahunty has argued that patterns of behavior may fit Egnor's beliefs but cannot establish divine authorship of moral convictions across persons.
Egnor offered no definition or evidence demonstrating God, relied on assertions and personal attacks, evaded proof through private relationship, and left divine hiddenness unanswered.
The closing directly addresses the debate's burden of proof and consolidates the con case that none of the presented Thomistic, moral, or personal arguments demonstrates God's existence.
Egnor's cumulative case for God and his criticisms of atheism, secular morality, scientific naturalism, and Dillahunty's understanding.
After extended questioning on morality, science, causation, and religious knowledge, Dillahunty receives a closing statement to assess the affirmative case as a whole.
Atheist objections fail because atheists do not rigorously understand arguments for God, evade the actual issues, and implausibly hold that everything arose from nothing without reason.
The closing presents Egnor's final defense of theism and rejection of atheism, directly framing the comparative adequacy of the positions on God's existence.
Dillahunty's closing claim that the affirmative supplied no definition, evidence, successful rebuttal, or demonstration that God exists.
Immediately after Dillahunty's closing rejection of the affirmative case, Egnor recounts investigating both sides after conversion and delivers his final assessment of atheism.
